ta-l1d42q2-d1e97.summary: The Prooemium of the second question of Distinction 42 turns to what is subject to divine power and announces three articles: whether God can do whatever is possible to another; whether he can do the impossible; and whether something should be judged simply possible or impossible by higher or lower causes.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e109.summary: First argument that God can do whatever is possible to another. All created power is modelled on his, as all good on his goodness, and what is in the copy is truer in the first exemplar.
claims: Created power copies divine power.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e112.summary: Second argument. The Philosopher says God and even the virtuous man can do evil things, and nothing is further from his power than evil.
claims: Aristotle: God can do evil.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e115.summary: Third argument. Will by its concept is free toward either alternative, and God most truly has will, so he can do good and evil.
claims: Will is free toward opposites.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e119.summary: Fourth argument. Nothing praiseworthy should be withheld from the great and highly praiseworthy, and being able to do evil and not doing it is praiseworthy (Sir. 31:10, 'he who could transgress and did not').
claims: Not sinning when able is praiseworthy.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e125.summary: Sed contra. As God cannot not be God, he cannot be imperfect, and creatures can do some things by weakness or imperfection, like suffering and dying.
claims: Creatures can suffer and die; God cannot.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e128.summary: Second sed contra. The supreme good cannot cause evil, as the supremely hot cannot cause cold, and creatures can do evil.
claims: The supreme good cannot cause evil.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e131.summary: Thomas's determination. Whatever perfection is in creatures is exemplarily drawn from the Creator's, but creatures have it less perfectly, so created power, insofar as it falls short of representing divine power, falls short of perfect ability, and what is attributed to it as participated at such a grade need not be attributed to divine power: as the stone's essence is modelled on God's yet God is not a stone, God's power is not a power of walking or suffering, as proximate principle of walking or suffering. The grades of powers, like natures, are ordered by divine disposition as they fall short of divine power more or less, so though no proper act of these powers at their determinate grades belongs to divine power as proximate principle, all their proper acts proceeding according to the order in which they are established reduce to God as first cause; so we do not say God can walk or suffer, but that he creates walking and suffering in others. Acts proceeding from determinate powers outside that order in no way reduce to divine causality, so we do not say he can sin or cause sin in others.
claims: God cannot do what creatures do by their limited grade (walk, suffer) but causes these acts as first cause.
Acts outside the order of powers, sins, are in no way from divine power.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e137.summary: Reply to the second argument. Some say 'evil things' is taken materially: God can do what are now evil things, which would not be evil if he did them. Or it is conditional, 'if he willed', whose antecedent and consequent are both impossible, which is not unfitting, like 'if a hundred are fewer than five, they are fewer than ten'.
claims: 'God can do evil' is material or a conditional with impossible antecedent.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e141.summary: Reply to the third argument. Being able to sin, according to Anselm and Boethius, does not belong to freedom of will but is a condition of a defectible will, as from nothing; freedom consists in being able to do or not do this, or do this or something else.
claims: Ability to sin is not part of freedom.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e144.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Something is praiseworthy in a lower nature that would be blameworthy in a higher, as ferocity is praiseworthy in a dog or lion but blameworthy in a man; so not sinning when able is a human's praise but would be blasphemy if said of God.
claims: Praise varies with nature.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e156.summary: First argument that God cannot do what is impossible to nature. The Commentator says every alteration is by a bodily agent, and God is incorporeal, so he can alter lower creatures only through the motion of the heavens, the first unaltered alterer, and through it nothing impossible to nature can occur.
claims: Alteration requires a bodily agent.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e159.summary: Second argument. All impossibility or necessity in propositions reduces to the first principle, that affirmation and negation cannot be simultaneously true, and God is said unable to make them true together, so he can do nothing impossible to nature.
claims: All impossibility reduces to non-contradiction.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e162.summary: Third argument. The per se impossible is more impossible than the per accidens impossible, and God cannot do the per accidens impossible, since he cannot make the past not to have been (Jerome: he cannot make a corrupted woman a virgin; Augustine; Agathon in the Philosopher), and the past not having been is impossible only per accidens, since before it happened it was contingent.
claims: God cannot change the past.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e172.summary: Fourth argument. God cannot act against the reasons he first implanted (Augustine), and as author of nature he does nothing against nature (Gloss on Rom. 11), and what is impossible to nature seems against nature.
claims: God does nothing against nature.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e175.summary: Sed contra. Whoever says 'all' excludes nothing, and the text says God can do all things.
claims: 'All things' excludes nothing.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e178.summary: Second sed contra. Hilary says God can do more than we can say (Dist. 19), and Luke 1:37 says no word is impossible with God, and we can say anything impossible, even that affirmation and negation hold together, as some philosophers did.
claims: Nothing is impossible with God.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e184.summary: Third sed contra. God and man differ more than two contraries, and God united human nature to divine, so he can much more make contraries be together, so affirmation and negation true together.
claims: The Incarnation unites greater opposites.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e187.summary: Fourth sed contra. As blindness is opposed to sight, virginity to conception, and God made a virgin conceive and be a mother while remaining a virgin, so he can make the blind see while remaining blind.
claims: Virgin birth parallels blind seeing.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e190.summary: Thomas's determination. 'Being able' implies a relation between the able and the possible, as knowing between knower and knowable, so ability can be denied on the side of the able or of the possible. No ability without imperfection is denied of God on his side, but defective ability, not pure ability but mixed with inability, is denied, since his power can have no defect, so it is not granted that he can sin. Sometimes ability is denied on the side of the possible, what can in no way have the character of possible, the per se impossible. Every power is to being or to non-being (as the power to corrupt), so what cannot have the character of being or non-being cannot be possible; so the same being and not being together is impossible in itself, since what is being and non-being is neither, and God is said unable to do it not by defect of power but because it falls short of the character of possible, as he is said not to know the false, which falls short of the knowable. So he cannot do anything implying contradiction: he cannot make the past not to have been, since what is necessarily is while it is and cannot then not be, and passes into the past with that necessity (Augustine: 'let God make what was done not to have been' means 'let what is true, by being true, not be'). So he cannot do anything where the opposite of the predicate is in the subject's definition (a man not rational, a triangle without three lines), nor make opposites together in the same thing, since one contrary's definition includes the other's privation, which includes negation. But whatever in itself does not conflict with the character of being or non-being God can do: that the heavens not be, another world, giving sight to the blind; these are impossible not in themselves but to something.
claims: God cannot do what implies contradiction, not from lack of power but because it is not possible.
He can do whatever does not conflict with being or non-being, even what is impossible to nature.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e197.summary: Reply to the first argument. It could be expounded as meaning this cannot happen by the order of natural operation, though it can by an agent above nature, were that not against the intention of the one who says it expressly of God, so on this he erred and his authority is not to be accepted; even philosophers teach the contrary, as Avicenna says matter obeys separate principles and their conceptions more than contrary natural agents. Whatever of others, it is most firmly to be held of God that he has not bound his power to the heavens.
claims: God's power is not bound to the heavens; Averroes erred.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e200.summary: Reply to the second argument. Something is impossible as it reduces to that principle: the per se impossible includes the principle in itself, and God cannot do it; what is impossible to something includes it in its order to that thing, as a dead man reviving: living is possible in itself, but a dead body has no power to produce it, so it is impossible; if it were posited to live by its own power, it would have both power and impotence for the same; nor does God do this in raising the dead, making the body live by its own power, but by a power he confers.
claims: Impossible to something differs from impossible per se; resurrection is by conferred power.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e203.summary: Reply to the third argument. The past not having been can be taken as per accidens or per se impossible. The thing called past, Socrates' running, is impossible only by its accident, pastness, outside its concept, and in itself is not impossible to God, who can make Socrates not run. Taken as under the accident of pastness, it is per se impossible, and God cannot do it, as 'Socrates not running while he runs' is impossible per se by the adjunct.
claims: The past is per se impossible to undo as past.
concepts: impossibile per accidens vs. per se

ta-l1d42q2-d1e206.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. God implanted in prime matter two kinds of reasons: causal or obediential reasons, by which all things are apt to obey God to become whatever pleases him, and seminal reasons, active principles by which natural effects are produced, against which he is sometimes said to act in miracles. Properly he acts not against them but beside or above them: above, producing an effect nature can in no way reach, like the form of glory in glorified bodies; beside, producing without natural causes an effect nature can produce, like turning water into wine (John 2). He does not act against them, since he neither does nor can make a natural active cause, remaining specifically the same, have another essential effect, which would be being the same and other; but he can destroy one nature and make another, removing one form and inducing another, as fire acts against air's nature in corrupting it.
claims: Miracles are above or beside nature, not against it.
Matter has obediential potency to whatever God wills.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e209.summary: Reply to the first sed contra. Only being or non-being can fall under the distribution of 'all', and what we said God cannot do is neither simply being nor non-being.
claims: The contradictory is not a 'thing'.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e212.summary: Reply to the second sed contra. Such impossibles, though uttered, cannot be conceived in the heart (Metaphysics 5), so they are not properly and perfectly words.
claims: Contradictions cannot be conceived.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e216.summary: Reply to the third sed contra. God did not join human nature to divine so as to be the same nature, or one person God and man in the same respect, but in different respects, and so he can undoubtedly join contraries in the same thing, as nature does too.
claims: The Incarnation unites natures in different respects.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e219.summary: Reply to the fourth sed contra. The cases differ: blindness is the privation of sight and includes its negation, so God cannot make one simultaneously blind and seeing; but virginity includes the negation not of motherhood but of union with a man.
claims: Virginity does not negate motherhood.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e231.summary: First argument that nothing should be judged simply impossible by lower causes. The Gloss on 1 Cor. 1:20 says God made the world's wisdom foolish, showing possible what it judged impossible, and the world's wisdom judges by lower causes.
claims: Worldly wisdom judges by lower causes.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e240.summary: Second argument. A lower cause cannot justify the wicked, yet we do not call this impossible, nor the world's coming to be before it was, which nature cannot do.
claims: Justification is not called impossible.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e243.summary: Third argument. Giving sight to the blind and conception to a virgin are impossible to nature, yet they could be and were done.
claims: Miracles happened.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e247.summary: Sed contra. Nothing is impossible with God (Luke 1), so if possibility were judged only by the higher cause, nothing would be impossible.
claims: Otherwise nothing would be impossible.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e250.summary: Second sed contra. Necessary and impossible are contraries, and something is not called necessary by the first cause's necessity (Dist. 38), or all would be necessary, so neither possible and impossible by higher causes.
claims: Modality follows proximate causes.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e253.summary: Thomas's determination. Something is impossible in itself, involving contradiction, judged impossible absolutely, not by relation to higher or lower causes. Something else is not impossible in itself but in relation to something, and here possible is said by active or passive potency, and either way something is called simply possible or impossible by comparison to its proximate active or material cause, whose conditions the effect follows: the remote matter of a statue is earth and water, the proximate bronze and wood, and we say a statue can be made from bronze but not from earth, since we call potential in something absolutely only what can be drawn from matter by one mover (Metaphysics 9). So all effects immediately from God, not through secondary causes (creation of the world and the soul, glorification), are judged possible or impossible by the higher, divine cause, though some can be judged possible by lower passive causes, as the soul relates to a body prepared by nature and grace to free choice. Effects naturally from lower proximate active and passive causes are judged possible or impossible by lower causes, as the blind seeing and the dead rising, since life and sight are immediate effects of lower causes, forms united to bodies.
claims: What is impossible in itself is impossible absolutely; otherwise possibility is judged by proximate causes.
Effects immediate from God are judged by him; effects naturally from lower causes are judged by them.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e256.summary: Reply to the first argument. Worldly wisdom was reckoned foolish because it judged what is impossible to nature so impossible that even God could not do it. Something can be called simply impossible that is possible to something, as something is called simply white that is not white in some part.
claims: Worldly wisdom erred in extending natural impossibility to God.

ta-l1d42q2-d1e269.summary: An expositio textus. (1) 'God could have made all things at once', not only all species but all individuals over all time, but reason prevented it, not by contrariety but by incompossibility, since God cannot make something not rational, so reason determines the work and power executes it. (2) 'Because this would not be of power but of weakness', as Dionysius says, with the example of calling something non-being: its very being is non-being, so being able to fall short of the perfectly possible is not simply ability. (3) Man or angel, however blessed, is not powerful 'of himself' or 'from himself': man can do nothing good of or from himself, since 'de' and 'ab' denote efficient cause, and what good he has he has from another; but 'per' denotes formal cause, so he can do some things per se, those completed by natural principles, and not others, those done by divine power like miracles; so the Son is said to do all things per se but not a se.
claims: God's power is executed according to his wisdom.
Creatures act per se but not a se.

ta-l1d42q2-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium announces three articles on what is subject to divine power: whether God can do whatever is possible to another, whether he can do the impossible, and by which causes possibility is judged.

ta-l1d42q2-Dd1e101.summary: Article 1 holds that God cannot do what creatures do by their limited grade, like walking or suffering, though he causes these acts as first cause, and that sins, outside the order of powers, are in no way from divine power. 'God can do evil' is material or conditional, ability to sin is not part of freedom, and not sinning when able is human, not divine, praise.
claims: God causes creaturely acts as first cause but cannot sin.

ta-l1d42q2-Dd1e148.summary: Article 2 holds that God can do whatever does not imply contradiction, even what is impossible to nature, but not the per se impossible, which is not a possible at all. So he cannot make the past not to have been. His power is not bound to the heavens, against Averroes. Miracles are above or beside nature, not against it, since matter has obediential potency, and the Incarnation and virgin birth involve no contradiction.
claims: Omnipotence extends to all that does not imply contradiction.
Miracles are above or beside nature.

ta-l1d42q2-Dd1e223.summary: Article 3 holds that what is impossible in itself is impossible absolutely, while relative possibility is judged by proximate causes. Effects immediate from God, like creation and glorification, are judged by him, and effects naturally from lower causes, like sight and life, by them. Worldly wisdom erred in making natural impossibility binding on God.
claims: Relative possibility follows proximate causes.

ta-l1d42q2-Dd1e264.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 42 explains that God's power executes what his wisdom determines, that ability to fail is not ability, and that creatures act per se but not a se.
claims: Power executes what wisdom determines.

ta-l1d42q2.summary: Quaestio 2 of Book I, Distinction 42 treats the objects of divine power. Article 1 holds that God causes creaturely acts as first cause but cannot do what belongs to limited natures or to sin. Article 2 holds that he can do whatever does not imply contradiction, including what is impossible to nature, but not the per se impossible, like undoing the past, and that miracles are above or beside nature, not against it. Article 3 holds that relative possibility is judged by proximate causes, and effects immediate from God by God.
claims: God can do all that does not imply contradiction.
He cannot sin or undo the past.
Miracles are above or beside nature.
